T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: PowerShell on scranton opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF from an unknown call-trace module during a hands-on-keyboard intrusion by pbeesly.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: New instance beyond the anchors: wsmprovhost.exe (pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff on nashua at 03:09:29, immediately before the PsExec/python delivery.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: SAM opened with 0xf003f by lsass.exe on scranton at 03:19:21-03:20:46; requester is lsass under the machine account, so attribution to the attacker is uncertain.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow usage, no ntds.dit writes, no shadow-copy service installs.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: Only LOCAL SERVICE querying Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC (routine machine-account secret read); no lsadump/secretsdump tooling.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No cachedump/dcc2/mscache tooling or SECURITY\Cache object access; NL$1 writes are normal OS cache maintenance.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: Single 4662 by NEWYORK$ machine account with DS-Replication-Get-Changes only (no Get-Changes-All), no drsuapi/dcsync tooling.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes' / 'trace stop' on scranton.dmevals.local, spawned exclusively by the signed Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe, Company 'Microsoft CoreXT', Networking-NetAnalytics) as part of Azure NetAnalytics telemetry, with a complete start/ETL-write/stop/merge lifecycle in C:\Windows\Temp. No attacker sniffing tooling or artifacts exist: zero hits for pktmon/dumpcap/tshark/wireshark/windump/rawcap/NetworkMiner/fiddler in Sysmon EID1 and Security 4688, zero pcap/npcap/winpcap/pktmon driver image loads (EID7), zero related registry writes (EID13), zero pcap service installs (7045), zero PowerShell script blocks referencing capture tooling, and the non-overlapping zeek window shows only ordinary service traffic with no capture-related notices.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: lsass handle traffic is mostly benign baseline (svchost 0x1000, Defender, Azure agents), but the same window contains PowerShell/wsmprovhost full-access lsass access and a remote thread into lsass — input/credential capture activity.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogger artifacts: keyboard registry writes are OS keyboard-layout/device keys; no SetWindowsHookEx/GetAsyncKeyState scripts, keylog services, or keyboard object handles.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Invoke-ScreenCapture script on scranton (pbeesly) loops CopyFromScreen every 300s saving desktop bitmaps to Downloads — GUI input capture.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No web content written to wwwroot/inetpub, no IIS/W3SVC service installs, no HTTP POSTs; the *login* PowerShell hit is file-collection/Compress-Archive staging.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: powershell.exe (PID 2976, pbeesly) opened lsass with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff and created a remote thread in lsass on scranton; wsmprovhost.exe did the same 0x1f3fff access on nashua — credential API hooking/injection.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625/4771/4740 events in windows.security and windows.other; the only 4776 is a successful validation (Status 0x0) for pbeesly. No repeated authentication attempts anywhere in the window.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons at all; the single runas invocation on scranton is a UAC elevation of hostui.exe, and PowerShell credential usage relies on hardcoded known secrets, not guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff and unbacked call trace, and LSA/SAM registry keys were accessed by attacker tooling — credential dumping/collection is present, but no offline cracking (no reg save, no hashcat/john/mimikatz) was observed.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625/4771 spray pattern; a single account (pbeesly) with one password was used against NASHUA via PsExec and Invoke-Command.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons and no user/password list processing; only a single hardcoded credential pair appears in PsExec command lines.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local a hidden, IEX-based PowerShell loader (PID 2976, launched by control.exe, decoding payload from monkey.png) opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16Z, and on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29Z — access to authentication/credential material consistent with MFA/credential interception. No MFA-provider registry or service tampering was observed (C120 zero hits), so the interception is at the credential-store level rather than via an installed MFA component.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: No forced-authentication artifacts: WebDAV HTTP methods are a legitimate Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/DavClnt upload of /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z from 10.0.1.4 to internal 192.168.0.4; SMB 445/139 is GPO/sysvol and IPC$ access from System; no .lnk/.scf/.url/.library-ms coercion files created; no WebDAV/NTLM/445 coercion in 4104 script blocks; all 4624 type-3 logons were Kerberos. Malicious PowerShell on scranton (steganography, hostui.exe persistence) is unrelated to T1187.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with full-access masks 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF from managed PowerShell call traces, embedded in a hands-on-keyboard intrusion by user pbeesly (obfuscated PowerShell, Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Exfil with hardcoded creds, sdelete64 wiping, PsExec64 with plaintext password to NASHUA). Other lsass full-access opens (csrss.exe, wininit.exe) and 0x1000/0x1400 opens by svchost/Azure agents are benign system behaviour.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No access to browser cookie/session stores was found: the only *cookies* file path in Sysmon was a LocalService INetCookies artefact created by svchost.exe; process access to Edge/Chrome images came only from Explorer.EXE/svchost.exe/ctfmon.exe with low GrantedAccess (0x1000/0x1400/0x2000); zero Security 4663/5145/4656 events referenced cookie or login-data files; and no 4104 script block contained cookie-extraction logic. The malicious-looking pbeesly activity (screen capture, 7z exfil to \\192.168.0.4\webdav, python.exe beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443) is collection/exfiltration, not web-session-cookie theft. Zeek (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and its HTTP POST check had zero hits.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Unsecured credentials harvested and staged: Draft.Zip of password/login-named files on scranton, working.zip on nashua, OfficeSupplies.7z exfiltrated to \\192.168.0.4\webdav.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Cleartext dmevals\pbeesly password in PsExec64 command line, hardcoded WebDAV credential cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd! in Invoke-Exfil, hardcoded RAR password fGzq5yKw on nashua, and a *pass*/*login*/*vpn* file-harvesting script on scranton.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: No reg save/query of SAM/SECURITY/LSA; the 17 credential-keyword registry writes are svchost/winlogon/lsass housekeeping.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: Zero hits for ConsoleHost_history, PSReadLine or history.txt across PowerShell, Sysmon and Security datasets.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificates via Export-PfxCertificate; Sysmon confirms C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: No Groups.xml/cpassword activity; SYSVOL DataStore writes are svchost.exe Group Policy client refresh on scranton and nashua.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Only the accesschk-created 'passwordsDB' artifact on scranton; no credential-store file reads were captured.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: accesschk.exe created C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB on scranton; no browser Login Data/cookie store access was observed in the window.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No cmdkey/vault/credman usage in process creation, 4688, script blocks or registry events; the nashua lsass 0x1F3FFF handle is a PowerShell remoting (wsmprovhost) session, and the scranton full-access lsass handle is reported under T1555.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: All password-manager checks (process creation, .kdbx/1password/keepass file creation, memory access, 4688, script blocks, windows.other) returned zero hits.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: A real intrusion by pbeesly (steganographic PowerShell from monkey.png, hidden/encoded PowerShell, hostui.exe UAC bypass, PSEXESVC+python.exe on nashua) coincides with full-access lsass handles (0x1FFFFF from PowerShell.exe on scranton, 0x1F3FFF from wsmprovhost.exe on nashua), but no authentication-process modification was observed.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: Logon process names are standard, the only machine-account 4648 is a routine taskhostw.exe self-logon, and lsass handle access is dominated by svchost.exe 0x1000 plus AV/telemetry 0x1400; no DC authentication patching.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No Notification Packages/PasswordFilter registry writes or 4657 events; the only 'password' file was accesschk.exe output passwordsDB, and no password-filter DLL loaded into lsass.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 events, no Set-ADAccountControl/Set-ADUser or reversible-encryption command lines; the single 4104 keyword hit was generic TimeSpan validation code.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739 or 5136 events; 4662 activity is LOCAL SERVICE reading $MACHINE.ACC, and the only AD-related processes were the Azure domain-join extension and cmd.exe.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory changes and no identity-sync/federation service installed; 7045 services were javamtsup.exe and PSEXESVC only.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider/Winlogon registry changes and only legitimate System32 network DLLs loaded; the lsass memory-write accesses are attributable to the credential-theft activity, not a network provider backdoor.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM/relay infrastructure, rogue TLS SNI or unusual Kerberos peer in windows.* or zeek; only PsExec/javamtsup lateral-movement tooling was found.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: SMB 445/139 connections are System->DC/file servers (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, link-local); no EnableMulticast change, no Responder/poisoning script blocks, no relayed NTLM logon.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: No unexpected gateway/duplicate-IP traffic pattern, no network-config tampering in object-access events, no ARP-poisoning tooling installed.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: Only local ipconfig.exe runs; no DHCP server/config events, no DHCP PowerShell, no UDP 67/68 traffic in zeek.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16 during a hands-on-keyboard session running Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-ScreenCapture and Invoke-SeaDukeStage; consistent with credential/ticket harvesting, though no ticket-theft artifact was directly observed.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: Only 3 krbtgt 4769 requests, all AES256 (0x12) with Failure Code 0x0 for pbeesly and SCRANTON$; no 4768/4771 anomalies, no golden-ticket tooling or script content.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: All 28 4769 service tickets are AES256 for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$, krbtgt); no forged service-ticket use or silver-ticket tooling observed.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No TGS requests for user-account SPNs and no RC4 tickets; 4648 events are pbeesly via PSEXESVC.exe (PsExec lateral movement), not roasting.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: No 4768 events in any Windows dataset and no asrep/GetNPUsers/Rubeus activity; zeek AS-REQs show KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED, i.e. pre-auth enforced.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential was directly observed, but the same pbeesly session on scranton.dmevals.local combined high-access lsass handle opens (0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF by PowerShell.exe) with explicit-credential logons and PsExec service installs on nashua.dmevals.local — credential-access/lateral-movement context around the certificate export.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only a benign LocalService INetCookies file creation by svchost.exe; no cookie-referencing PowerShell script blocks and no external web destinations in Zeek.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Certificate private keys exported to a password-protected .pfx on scranton, enabling SAML/token forgery with the stolen key material.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: 6 planned checks, all with zero hits

T1649.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificates to C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx with password 'saribas' on scranton at 03:04:57.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on SCRANTON
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:04:56 UTC (23:04:56 local) on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block (4104, ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) defining function Get-PrivateKeys. The script enumerates every certificate in cert:\LocalMachine recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for each one that has a Thumbprint, writing to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. One second later (03:04:57.460 UTC) Sysmon recorded powershell.exe (PID 3876) creating C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx, confirming the export actually ran and private keys were written to disk in exportable form. A companion script block at 03:08:51 (Invoke-BeachCleanup, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) deletes $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.pfx along with *.bmp, *.png and %APPDATA%\OfficeSupplies.7z, i.e. anti-forensic cleanup of the stolen certificate bundles and staged data. This is textbook T1649 certificate theft: harvesting machine private keys for later authentication/forgery. The same actor then used PsExec64.exe from SCRANTON with cleartext credentials (dmevals\pbeesly) to run C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on \\NASHUA at 03:11-03:14, consistent with using harvested material to move laterally.

findings.summary: Hunted all four Windows hosts (2020-05-02 02:55–03:28Z) for T1539. No event shows a non-browser process reading a browser cookie database or browser memory for session theft. (1) Sysmon file-create (event 2) stacking returned only OS/AppX artefacts (USOPrivate update store, ContentDeliveryManager creatives, Cortana caches, systemprofile AppData blobs) — no Cookies/Login Data/Web Data files. (2) A targeted ES|QL search for file paths matching *cookies*/*login data*/*web data*/*cookies.sqlite* returned exactly one hit: svchost.exe creating C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\...\AC\INetCookies, a normal Windows service-profile artefact. (3) Process-access (event 10) to Edge/Chrome/Firefox images came only from Explorer.EXE, svchost.exe and ctfmon.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000/0x1400/0x2000 (query-limited/read-small), i.e. normal shell/COM/UI automation, not full-access (0x1fffff/0x1410) reads typical of cookie stealers. (4) Security 4663/5145/4656 events referencing cookie stores: zero. (5) The 4104 script blocks matching *cookie*/*session*/*token*/*browser* were benign module manifests/localized strings on newyork (SYSTEM) plus pbeesly's CIM-session aliases and a Get-Process -IncludeUserName session enumeration on scranton/nashua — no cookie extraction code. (6) The suspicious pbeesly activity on scranton (Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil with 7Zip4Powershell and a WebDAV copy to \\192.168.0.4\webdav) and the PyInstaller python.exe on nashua beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443 are collection/exfiltration tradecraft, not web-session-cookie theft. Zeek data (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and its POST check returned zero hits, so no HTTP cookie exfil is observable.

findings.summary: No reg.exe/reg query/reg save of SAM, SECURITY or LSA keys was found (C159 zero hits; C147 zero hits for reg save/ntdsutil/vssadmin). The 17 registry value-set events matching credential keywords are all routine: svchost.exe writing IdentityCRL ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups policy values on nashua and scranton, winlogon.exe writing PUUActive/DP and PasswordExpiryNotification values for the pbeesly profile, and lsass.exe writing its own Lsa\LsaPid/LsaCfgFlagsDefault/ProductType values during a reboot at 03:19:09Z. No attacker process touched credential-bearing registry keys.
findings.title: Registry credential-key access not observed; only OS/winlogon housekeeping writes

findings.summary: Checks C163/C164/C165/C166 for ConsoleHost_history, PSReadLine and history.txt returned zero hits, and a broader ES|QL sweep of Sysmon process creations for 'history' returned no matching command lines. The only PowerShell script blocks referencing credentials are the attacker's own Get-PrivateKeys/Invoke-Exfil functions, not reads of shell history files.
findings.title: No shell-history or PSReadLine harvesting observed

findings.summary: C171-C174 (Groups.xml, cpassword, gpprefdecrypt, SYSVOL in command lines) had zero hits. The 22 Sysmon file-create events under C:\Windows\System32\GroupPolicy\DataStore\0\sysvol\dmevals.local\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9} (gpt.ini, Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf) were all written by svchost.exe on scranton (03:01:43Z, 03:19:18Z) and nashua (03:10:40Z) — the standard Group Policy client caching its local DataStore, with no Groups.xml and no attacker process involved.
findings.title: SYSVOL/GPP file creation is normal Group Policy client refresh, not cpassword harvesting
No browser credential-store access observed
findings.summary: No evidence of browser credential theft. The only file-creation event matching browser store names in the whole window is a single svchost.exe write to C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-...\AC\INetCookies on scranton at 03:21:05Z, which is a normal Windows service-profile cookie container, not a user browser profile. No process accessed chrome.exe/firefox.exe/msedge.exe memory, no 4663 object access on 'Login Data'/'logins.json'/'key4.db'/'Web Data', and no command line or script block referenced those files. The attacker's PowerShell collection script on scranton did enumerate files matching *pass*, *login*, *vpn* etc. for archiving, but that is file collection, not extraction of browser password stores.

findings.title: No Windows Credential Manager / vault access; LSASS access on nashua is PowerShell remoting
findings.summary: No cmdkey, vaultcmd, credman or Credential Manager API usage was found in process creation, 4688, script blocks or registry events (checks C186/C188/C189 zero hits). The 0x1F3FFF lsass handle on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z came from wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) with a CallTrace through System.ni.dll and Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll — i.e. a PowerShell remoting session, not a credential dump; nashua also shows PSEXESVC.exe spawning C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe repeatedly (03:11–03:15) and Rar.exe archiving to working.zip, which is lateral movement/collection rather than Credential Manager theft. The scranton PowerShell→lsass full-access handle is reported under T1555. The only 'Credential' string in windows.other is a benign Credential Guard configuration message (event 14) on scranton.

findings.title: No password-manager store access observed
findings.summary: All password-manager checks returned zero hits: no process creation, file creation (.kdbx/1password/keepass), process-memory access to KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden, 4688 command lines, script blocks or windows.other messages referencing password managers. The only password-like artefacts are the attacker's own hardcoded credentials in scripts (e.g. 'MyCozyPassw0rd!' in Invoke-Exfil and 'saribas' used as the .pfx export password), which are attacker tooling, not theft from a password manager.

findings.summary: Handle access to lsass.exe (326 events) is dominated by svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (286) plus AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe with 0x1400 — normal security-product/telemetry query access. The non-standard full-access opens (PowerShell.exe 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF, wsmprovhost.exe 0x1F3FFF) are credential-theft style reads, not modification of DC authentication. Logon process names for 4624/4648 are standard (Kerberos 217, Advapi 76, User32 2, NtLmSsp 1); the single 4648 with a machine-account target is SCRANTON$ logging on to scranton$ from taskhostw.exe, a routine scheduled-task style self-logon. No cryptdll/ntds DLL loads into unexpected processes and no lsass/cryptdll messages in windows.other.
findings.title: No domain-controller authentication tampering; lsass handle access is from PowerShell hosts, not DC auth patching

findings.summary: The only file matching the password/filter pattern was C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB, created by C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\accesschk.exe on scranton at 03:04:35 — an admin tool output file, not a DLL. The remaining matches are Cortana filtertrie cache files under pbeesly's profile. No registry writes to Notification Packages/PasswordFilter/Lsa, no 4657 on those keys, no PowerShell referencing them, and the only lsass image load was lsass.exe itself.
findings.title: No password-filter DLL registration or load into lsass

findings.summary: No 4739 events exist in windows.security, no process command lines reference Reversible/Set-ADAccountControl/Set-ADUser, and no windows.other messages mention reversible encryption. The single PowerShell 4104 hit for the reversible-encryption keywords was a false positive: a SYSTEM script block on newyork.dmevals.local containing generic TimeSpan validation code, not an AD account-control change.
findings.title: No reversible-encryption account control changes

findings.summary: No 4739 events, no 5136 directory-service changes, and the only 4662 objects were SecretObject reads of Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC by LOCAL SERVICE (normal LSA secret access) plus one NEWYORK$ read. The two processes matching ADUser/AuthenticationPolicy command lines were the Azure JsonADDomainExtension.exe domain-join extension and cmd.exe. Newly installed services (7045) were Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service (javamtsup.exe) on scranton and repeated PSEXESVC installs on nashua by pbeesly — lateral-movement tooling, not an authentication bypass component.
findings.title: No MFA/authentication-policy modification

findings.summary: No 5136 directory modifications were recorded, and the 7045 service installations in the window are javamtsup.exe and PSEXESVC — no AAD Connect, federation or identity-sync service was installed or modified. The 20,259 image-load events are overwhelmingly standard System32 DLLs (ntdll, KernelBase, kernel32, rpcrt4, sechost); no anomalous DLL was loaded into an identity process.
findings.title: No hybrid-identity / federation or sync-service backdooring

findings.summary: Across windows.sysmon/security/other/powershell (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) and zeek (2020-04-30 00:06-00:45Z) no AiTM tooling, rogue relay endpoint or interception infrastructure was found. Outbound connections (1229 event.code 3) are dominated by internal hosts 192.168.0.4, 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.4/5/6 and Microsoft/Office telemetry addresses; DNS queries (81 event.code 22) are ordinary AD/DC SRV lookups and Microsoft domains. The only new services are javamtsup (scranton) and PSEXESVC (nashua), i.e. lateral-movement tooling rather than interception. Zeek TLS SNI is uniformly 192.168.0.4 and Kerberos peers are all 10.0.0.4 (the DC), with no rogue KDC/relay peer.
findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity observed; credential theft on hosts was done with PsExec + python.exe, not interception

findings.summary: All 66 SMB (445/139) connections in windows.sysmon come from process 'System' on newyork/scranton/nashua/utica toward 10.0.0.4 (DC), 10.0.1.6 and the link-local fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 - consistent with normal domain authentication/file access, not a relay target. No 4657 change to EnableMulticast and no PowerShell script block referencing Responder/EnableMulticast (checks C243/C244 zero hits). The 4697 service installs are javamtsup (scranton, pbeesly) and PSEXESVC (nashua, pbeesly) plus a burst of per-user svchost services on scranton at 03:20:48 - lateral movement, not name-resolution poisoning. The single NTLM network logon (4624 type 3, NtLmSsp, pbeesly, source 172.18.39.2, workstation 10.0.1.4) on scranton at 03:20:41 is a direct NTLM authentication, not a relayed one.
findings.title: SMB traffic is normal DC/file-server access; no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay tooling

findings.summary: Outbound connection stacking shows no unexpected gateway or duplicate-IP pattern that would suggest ARP poisoning: destinations are the internal DC/file servers (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.4/5/6, 192.168.0.4) plus Microsoft cloud ranges. DNS queries are normal AD SRV/DC discovery and Microsoft telemetry; zeek DNS responses are 25 NOERROR / 12 NXDOMAIN with no anomalous answers. Object-access stacking (10834 events) shows only routine registry/LSA/Winlogon reads and Defender definition files - no network-configuration tampering. No ARP-poisoning tooling was installed (only javamtsup and PSEXESVC services).
findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning indicators; traffic paths and DNS answers are consistent

findings.summary: The only DHCP-related process activity is 3 executions of C:\Windows\System32\ipconfig.exe (local interface inspection), with no DHCP server/service installation, no DHCP configuration events (1341/1342/1020/1063 zero hits), no PowerShell DHCP/rogue-server script blocks and no Zeek conn traffic to UDP 67/68. Logon process stacking for 4624 is Kerberos (217), Advapi (76), User32 (2) and one NtLmSsp - no evidence of credentials captured via a spoofed DHCP/rogue gateway.
findings.title: No DHCP spoofing: only local ipconfig queries, no rogue DHCP server or DHCP config changes
No golden-ticket indicators: krbtgt service tickets are ordinary AES256 TGT renewals for pbeesly/SCRANTON$
findings.summary: The 4769 events on newyork.dmevals.local include 3 krbtgt service-ticket requests (1 for pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL, 2 for SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL), all with Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 (AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96), Ticket Options 0x60810010 and Failure Code 0x0 — normal TGT renewal/forwardable-ticket behaviour, not RC4 (0x17) or forged-ticket patterns. No 4768/4771/4770 anomalies, no krbtgt/golden/mimikatz/kirbi strings in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, and no mimikatz/Rubeus command lines in Sysmon. The high-privilege LSASS access on SCRANTON is reported under T1558 as suspicious, but nothing in the retrieved data shows a forged TGT being used.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators: all 4769 service tickets are AES256 for machine accounts, no forged service-ticket use
findings.summary: All 28 4769 events in windows.security are AES256 (0x12) service-ticket requests for machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 11, NASHUA$ 10, SCRANTON$ 3, krbtgt 3, WEC$ 1) with Failure Code 0x0; none target a user account SPN and none show RC4 or anomalous encryption. 4672 special-privilege logons are dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SYSTEM 54, pbeesly 17) with no unusual account receiving sensitive privileges. No silver/ticket/mimikatz/kirbi strings in PowerShell script blocks. The suspicious LSASS access on SCRANTON is captured under T1558; no evidence of forged service tickets was retrieved.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 TGS requests for user SPNs, no roasting tooling; 4648 events are PsExec-driven lateral movement by pbeesly
findings.summary: Kerberoasting requires TGS requests for user-account SPNs, typically RC4 (0x17). All 28 4769 events are AES256 (0x12) and target only machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$, krbtgt) — no user SPN was requested. No kerberoast/SPN/Invoke-Kerberoast/GetUserSPNs strings in PowerShell 4104 blocks and no roasting tool command lines in Sysmon. The 15 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly authenticating via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local (Target Server Name 'localhost') and from scranton.dmevals.local, plus routine DWM-1/UMFD-0/UMFD-1/UMFD-2/SCRANTON$ winlogon/wininit/taskhostw events — consistent with PsExec lateral movement, not credential roasting. Zeek kerberos records (separate 2020-04-30 window) show only pbeesly AS/TGS for krbtgt and cifs/host/ldap/HTTP services in AES256, with KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED on the initial AS-REQ (normal pre-auth).

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting: no 4768 events, no GetNPUsers/Rubeus/asrep activity
findings.summary: AS-REP roasting requires AS-REQ (4768) for accounts without pre-authentication. No 4768 events exist in windows.other or windows.security, no asrep/GetNPUsers/rubeus/preauth strings appear in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, and no matching command lines appear in Sysmon process creation (0 hits). The only AS-REQ activity is in the non-overlapping zeek window (2020-04-30) for pbeesly, where the initial AS-REQ returns KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED — i.e. pre-authentication is enforced, the opposite of a roastable account.

findings.title: No browser cookie theft or forged-cookie replay observed
findings.summary: The only cookie-related file event in the window is a single Sysmon file-create of C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies by svchost.exe on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:21:05Z, which is normal LocalService package/AppContainer cookie-store activity, not access to a user browser cookie database. No PowerShell script block referencing cookies was found (zero hits), and the Zeek HTTP/TLS data (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) shows only a single internal destination 192.168.0.4 with no external web identity service. Nothing indicates cookie theft or forged web cookies.

findings.title: ROOT certificate store blob modified on NASHUA by Sysmon.exe (likely benign tooling artifact)
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02 03:16:19 UTC, security event 4657 shows the 'Blob' value of \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656 being modified by process C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe under NASHUA$ (SYSTEM, logon 0x3e7). This is the only certificate-store registry write in the dataset and it is a single event, not a pattern of rogue root CA installation; the writing image is the Sysmon binary path rather than a certificate utility, and the old/new values are not auditable for REG_BINARY. It does not show an attacker adding a forged trust anchor, so I treat it as a benign/ambiguous artifact rather than evidence of certificate forgery. The genuine T1649 activity in this window is the private-key export on SCRANTON.

incidents.title: Hidden PowerShell opens LSASS with full-access masks and injects a remote thread on scranton
incidents.rationale: All describe the same event: PowerShell.exe PID 2976 (pbeesly) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF and a CreateRemoteThread with an UNKNOWN call trace at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z — LSASS memory access consistent with credential dumping.

incidents.title: wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opens LSASS with 0x1F3FFF during pbeesly remote PowerShell session
incidents.rationale: Same event on nashua.dmevals.local: wsmprovhost.exe PID 7720 opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF via the PowerShell Management module during pbeesly's Invoke-Command session; LSASS access, though the call trace suggests a PowerShell cmdlet.

incidents.title: SAM hive opened with 0xf003f by lsass on scranton
incidents.rationale: lsass.exe opened the SAM registry object with 0xf003f during the intrusion window — consistent with local account hash access, though possibly legitimate system activity.

incidents.title: Invoke-ScreenCapture loop capturing the desktop every 300s on scranton
incidents.rationale: PowerShell script block on scranton defines Invoke-ScreenCapture using Graphics.CopyFromScreen to save full-screen bitmaps every 300 seconds — GUI input capture.

incidents.title: Credential-harvesting chain on scranton with pfx export, staging, and PsExec lateral use of pbeesly credentials
incidents.rationale: Broader unsecured-credentials activity by pbeesly on scranton (Get-PrivateKeys export, Invoke-Exfil staging, javamtsup.exe service) followed by PsExec to nashua — unsecured credentials.

incidents.title: Hardcoded plaintext credentials in attacker PowerShell scripts and staged archive
incidents.rationale: Same script blocks on scranton embed plaintext credentials: pfx password 'saribas' and WebDAV account cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd! in Invoke-Exfil (psversion.ps1) — credentials in files.

incidents.title: PsExec on scranton launches python.exe on nashua with plaintext pbeesly password
incidents.rationale: PsExec64.exe command line on scranton carries cleartext domain credential '-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by' to start python.exe on NASHUA — credentials in files/command line.

incidents.title: Password-protected archive staged on nashua with hardcoded RAR password
incidents.rationale: Rar.exe on nashua run with hardcoded archive password '-hpfGzq5yKw' to create working.zip, then wiped with sdelete64 — credentials in files.

incidents.title: Credential-harvesting script on scranton collects password/login-named files into an archive
incidents.rationale: PowerShell on scranton enumerated the user profile for *pass*, *login*, *vpn*, *sifr* and similar files and compressed them into Draft.Zip — credentials in files.

incidents.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on scranton
incidents.rationale: Same script block (Get-PrivateKeys, readme.ps1, pbeesly, 03:04:56Z) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and exporting every certificate with its private key via Export-PfxCertificate to Downloads\<random>.pfx — private key theft.

incidents.title: accesschk.exe on scranton probes a 'passwordsDB' file in the Sysinternals folder
incidents.rationale: accesschk.exe from the attacker-staged SysinternalsSuite created passwordsDB, indicating a password store being touched; no browser credential database access observed.

incidents.title: Credential-access intrusion on scranton/nashua without authentication-process modification
No malicious network provider DLL; LSASS memory-write access is the credential-theft signal
Hidden PowerShell compiles .NET payloads with csc.exe from Temp response files on scranton
incidents.rationale: csc.exe compiling DLLs from Temp response files under hidden PowerShell is obfuscated/compiled payload execution, not credential access.

incidents.title: PsExec-delivered python.exe on nashua beacons to 192.168.0.4:8443 and spawns cmd/powershell
incidents.rationale: PyInstaller python.exe on nashua making 348 outbound connections to 192.168.0.4:8443 and spawning cmd/powershell is command-and-control/remote control, not credential access.

incidents.title: Screensaver-named loader in C:\ProgramData\victim opens LSA registry key and stages IEX payload on scranton
incidents.rationale: explorer.exe launched a .scr loader that opened the LSA registry key, spawned cmd.exe, and wrote monkey.png for the hidden PowerShell stager — user execution of a malicious file, not itself credential access.

incidents.title: hostui.exe launched with -verb runas and hostui.lnk placed in StartUp for persistence on scranton
incidents.rationale: Elevation via -verb runas and a StartUp-folder shortcut are privilege escalation/persistence, not credential access.

incidents.title: sdclt.exe UAC-bypass-style launches from cmd.exe in C:\ProgramData\victim on scranton
incidents.rationale: sdclt.exe launched from cmd.exe is a UAC-bypass attempt (bypass user account control), not credential access.
